e.etymology: An Italian elaboration of Romana, woman of Rome, from Latin Romanus. It spread through Spanish-speaking countries in the late 20th century.
The Swahili form of Omar, from Arabic Umar, tied to a root meaning to live long or flourish. It is common in East Africa and among African American families.

e.meaning: short form of Wilhelmina; in Sanskrit, fish
e.etymology: Historically a short form of Wilhelmina and other names ending in -mina. Unrelated names share the spelling: Sanskrit Mina, fish, Persian and Arabic Mina, and Japanese and Korean names written with various characters.
namesakes: Mina Harker (heroine of Bram Stoker's Dracula)

assoc.t: Mina Harker, heroine of Bram Stoker's Dracula

e.etymology: From the Roman name Maximilianus, a derivative of Maximus, greatest. Emperor Frederick III chose it for his son in 1459, and it became a favorite of German and Austrian royalty.
From Sanskrit arjuna, bright, white or silver. Arjuna is the great archer of the Mahabharata, to whom Krishna speaks the Bhagavad Gita.

assoc.t: Arjuna, archer hero of the Mahabharata

e.meaning: from English place names: leek garden or farm by a stream
e.etymology: From an English surname taken from several places named Layton or Leighton, Old English for a leek garden or a farm by a watercourse.

assoc.t: Professor Layton, puzzle-solving video game hero
Layton, Utah, city north of Salt Lake City

e.etymology: A spelling of Kaylee, a late 20th-century combination of Kay and Lee. The -leigh spelling took off in Britain after the 1985 Marillion song Kayleigh.
namesakes: Kayleigh McEnany (former White House press secretary)

e.etymology: From Arabic hamza, an epithet for the lion, from a root meaning strong or steadfast. Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, an uncle of Muhammad, was famed for his courage in battle.

assoc.t: hamza, the Arabic sign for a glottal stop

e.etymology: The Russian form of Nicholas, from Greek Nikolaos, built from nike, victory, and laos, people.
namesakes: Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov (composer of Flight of the Bumblebee)

e.meaning: in Japanese, often wise or healthy plus three (third son)
e.etymology: A Japanese name written with various characters, commonly ken, wise or healthy, plus zo, three, a traditional ending for a third son. Designer Kenzo Takada made it known in the West.

assoc.t: Kenzo, Paris fashion and fragrance house

e.etymology: A pet form of India, Indigo or Indiana, given on its own since the 2010s. It also matches the word indie, short for independent, as in indie music and film.

assoc.t: indie, short for independent music, film and games
Indy, nickname of Indiana Jones (same sound)
Indy 500 auto race (same sound)

e.meaning: short form of names ending in -lina, such as Carolina
e.etymology: A short form of names ending in -lina, such as Carolina, Angelina and Paulina, used on its own since the 1800s. An unrelated Arabic name Lina is often glossed as tender.

e.meaning: Spanish form of James and Jacob, supplanter
e.etymology: The Spanish and Portuguese form of James, from Late Latin Iacomus, a variant of Iacobus (Jacob), from Hebrew Ya'aqov. In English it is also a spelling of Jamie, used for girls.
namesakes: Jaime Lannister (knight in Game of Thrones)
Jaime Pressly (actress, My Name Is Earl)

assoc.t: Jaime Lannister, the Kingslayer of Game of Thrones

e.etymology: The Scandinavian and Dutch short form of Johannes (John), from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. In the US it is also popular with Spanish-speaking families.
Coined by Shakespeare for Prospero's daughter in The Tempest, from Latin mirandus, admirable or to be wondered at.
namesakes: Miranda Priestly (editor in The Devil Wears Prada)

assoc.t: Miranda rights, the warning police read at arrest
Hamilton creator Lin-Manuel Miranda
Miranda, a moon of Uranus
Miranda, Prospero's daughter in The Tempest

e.etymology: From Arabic rayyan, well-watered or luxuriant. In Islamic tradition, Ar-Rayyan is the gate of paradise reserved for those who fast.
From the Irish surname O Madadhain, descendant of Madadhan, a pet form of madadh, dog or hound.

assoc.t: Madden NFL, EA's football video game series
NFL coach and broadcaster John Madden
Steve Madden shoes

e.etymology: A spelling of Cataleya, taken from the Cattleya orchid, a tropical flower named for English horticulturist William Cattley. The 2011 film Colombiana, whose heroine is named Cataleya, launched it as a given name.

assoc.t: Cataleya, Zoe Saldana's assassin in Colombiana

e.etymology: A modern name used mainly in Mexican American families and related to Yaritza. It is often said to be of Nahuatl (Aztec) origin, but that derivation is not well documented.

e.meaning: Greek mother goddess; perhaps from words for flow or earth
e.etymology: From Rhea, the Titan mother of Zeus and the Olympian gods. The origin of her name is disputed; proposals include Greek rheo, to flow, and era, earth.

assoc.t: Titan mother of the Olympian gods in Greek myth
rhea, a large flightless South American bird
Rhea, a moon of Saturn

e.note: Rhymes with the end of diarrhea, which can invite teasing.

e.etymology: From Hebrew hadas, myrtle. In the Book of Esther it is the Hebrew name of Queen Esther.

assoc.t: Hadassah, the American Jewish women's organization

e.etymology: From the Irish surname O Sluaghadhain, descendant of Sluaghadhan, a name from sluaghadh, a raid or military expedition.

assoc.t: Sloan Kettering cancer center and MIT Sloan School

e.etymology: From the surname given to someone from Scotland. Old English Scottas, from Late Latin Scotti, first meant the Gaels of Ireland, who later settled Scotland.
namesakes: F. Scott Fitzgerald (author of The Great Gatsby)
Scott Pilgrim (comic book and film hero)

assoc.t: Scott paper towels and toilet paper
Great Scott!, an old exclamation of surprise

e.meaning: pet form of Jean, Jessica or Jesse
e.etymology: For girls, a Scottish pet form of Jean and Janet and later a short form of Jessica. For boys, a variant of Jesse, from Hebrew Yishai, the father of King David.

assoc.t: Jessie the yodeling cowgirl in Toy Story
Jessie's Girl, Rick Springfield's 1981 hit song
Jessie, Disney Channel sitcom about a nanny

e.meaning: traditionally Botolph's town or Botolph's stone
e.etymology: From the Massachusetts capital, named after Boston in Lincolnshire, England. The English town's name is traditionally explained as Botolph's town or Botolph's stone, though this is uncertain.

assoc.t: capital of Massachusetts
Boston, the rock band behind More Than a Feeling

e.etymology: A modern spelling of Camden, an English surname and place name, probably Old English for an enclosed valley.
From a Spanish and Portuguese surname and place name, a contraction of Santa Ana, Saint Anne.

assoc.t: guitarist Carlos Santana and his rock band
Santana Lopez of the TV series Glee

e.etymology: From the Spanish word reina, queen, from Latin regina. Reina is also a Japanese girls' name written with various characters.

e.meaning: pet form of Eleanor, Ellen and Helen
e.etymology: A pet form of Eleanor, Ellen and Helen, with an N carried over from the old endearment mine Ellen. It was a popular given name in its own right around 1900.
namesakes: Nellie Oleson (mean girl of Little House on the Prairie)

assoc.t: rapper Nelly (same sound)
Whoa, Nellie!, an old expression of surprise

e.etymology: The French form of Anna, from Hebrew Channah (Hannah), grace or favor. It honors Saint Anne, by tradition the mother of the Virgin Mary.
namesakes: Anne Frank (teenage diarist of the Holocaust)
Anne Shirley (heroine of Anne of Green Gables)

assoc.t: Anne Shirley of Anne of Green Gables
Anne Frank, diarist and Holocaust victim
Auntie Anne's, mall pretzel chain

e.meaning: pet form of Charles and Charlotte, free man
e.etymology: An older spelling of Charlie, the pet form of Charles and Charlotte, from the Germanic word karl, free man. Common for boys in the 1880s, it is now given mostly to girls.

assoc.t: charley horse, a sudden muscle cramp
Hurricane Charley, which hit southwest Florida in 2004

e.etymology: A spelling of Isaiah, from Hebrew Yeshayahu, Yahweh is salvation, the name of the major Old Testament prophet.
